provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify key concepts from SSS two Geography curriculum.
The students should be able to answer quiz questions on previous topics.
Introduction:
We have completed our SSS two Geography studies and now we need to refresh our memory before moving to new topics. This revision will help us build a strong foundation for our final year.
Content:
We will review map work basics including scale, direction, and symbols. We will also revisit important topics like rocks, weathering, and landforms. Students should recall how to interpret topographical maps and identify various geographical features. We will discuss examples of Nigerian landforms like the Jos Plateau and Niger Delta.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to complete a map interpretation exercise using a topographical map of Nigeria.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the importance of map symbols in Geography?
2. List three types of rocks found in Nigeria.
3. Explain the process of mechanical weathering with a local example.
Summary:
Today's revision has helped us consolidate our knowledge from SSS two and prepare for more advanced topics in our final year.

topics.title: The earth as a planet
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the earth's movements and their effects.
The students should be able to solve exam questions related to earth movements.
Introduction:
Building on our previous knowledge of the solar system, we will now focus specifically on our planet Earth and its unique characteristics and movements.
Content:
The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours causing day and night. It also revolves around the sun once every 365.25 days creating our year and seasons. The 23.5-degree tilt of Earth's axis is responsible for the variation in sunlight received, which creates seasons. In Nigeria, we experience two main seasons: the rainy season (April to October) and the dry season (November to March). The Harmattan wind, characterized by dry dusty air from the Sahara, occurs during the dry season.
Class activity:
Students will create a model showing Earth's rotation and revolution using simple materials to demonstrate day/night and seasons.
Evaluation questions:
1. State two effects of the Earth's rotation.
2. Explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes seasons.
3. Describe the Harmattan season in Nigeria.
4. Calculate the local time if it is 12 noon at Greenwich (0°) and the location is 30°E.
Summary:
Understanding Earth's movements helps us explain various natural phenomena including seasons, time differences, and climate patterns that affect our daily lives in Nigeria.

topics.title: Rocks
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between the three main types of rocks.
The students should be able to list uses of different rocks in Nigeria.
Introduction:
We have previously studied the structure of the Earth, and now we will examine the rocks that make up the Earth's crust, focusing on their types, characteristics, and economic importance.
Content:
There are three main types of rocks: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Igneous rocks are formed from cooled magma or lava, like granite and basalt found in Jos. Sedimentary rocks are formed from accumulated sediments over time, such as sandstone and limestone used in building our houses. Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure, like marble and schist. Rocks in Nigeria have various economic uses - limestone for cement production at Obajana, coal for electricity generation at Enugu, and granite for construction across the country.
Class activity:
Students will collect different rock samples (if available) or observe images to identify and classify them into the three rock types.
Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between igneous and sedimentary rocks.
2. List three metamorphic rocks and their uses.
3. Explain how sedimentary rocks are formed.
4. Identify one major rock deposit in Nigeria and its economic importance.
Summary:
Understanding rock types helps us identify valuable mineral resources that contribute to Nigeria's economy and development.

topics.title: Plate tectonics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the process of folding and faulting.
The students should be able to identify landforms resulting from tectonic activities.
Introduction:
Building on our knowledge of rocks, we will now explore how the Earth's crust is divided into plates and how their movement creates various landforms through folding and faulting processes.
Content:
The Earth's crust is divided into large plates that move slowly. When these plates collide, they can fold and buckle, forming mountains. The folding process creates anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds). Faulting occurs when rocks break and move along fractures, creating fault scarps, rift valleys, and block mountains. In Nigeria, the Jos Plateau was formed by volcanic activity and uplifting, while the Benue Trough is a rift valley formed by tension forces. The Eastern Highlands with features like the Obudu Plateau show evidence of tectonic activities.
Class activity:
Students will create models of folded and faulted landforms using clay or paper to demonstrate how these processes create different features.
Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the difference between folding and faulting.
2. List three landforms produced by tectonic activities.
3. Describe how the Jos Plateau was formed.
4. Differentiate between anticlines and synclines.
Summary:
Plate tectonic processes have shaped Nigeria's landscape over millions of years, creating the diverse landforms we see today.

topics.title: Volcanicity
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify volcanic landforms and features.
The students should be able to explain the effects of volcanic activity.
Introduction:
Following our study of plate tectonics, we will now focus specifically on volcanic activity, examining the processes, landforms created, and their effects on the environment and human activities.
Content:
Volcanicity refers to the movement of molten rock (magma) from beneath the Earth's crust to the surface. This process creates various landforms including volcanic mountains, lava plateaus, and calderas. In Nigeria, volcanic activity is not currently active, but evidence of past volcanicity can be seen in the Jos Plateau with features like the Jos Plateau itself being volcanic in origin. Volcanic rocks like basalt are found in areas like Biu in Borno State. The effects of volcanicity include the creation of fertile soil ideal for agriculture, the formation of geothermal energy sources, and the potential for destruction through eruptions.
Class activity:
Students will research and present on a major volcanic eruption and its effects on the environment and human population.
Evaluation questions:
1. List three volcanic landforms.
2. Explain how volcanic activity can be beneficial to humans.
3. Describe the volcanic features found in the Jos Plateau.
4. Differentiate between magma and lava.
Summary:
Volcanicity, though not currently active in Nigeria, has played a significant role in shaping parts of our country's landscape and continues to influence geological processes.

topics.title: Weathering and erosion
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the processes of weathering and erosion.
The students should be able to identify landforms created by these processes.
Introduction:
We have studied how rocks are formed and how tectonic forces create landforms. Now we will examine how these rocks and landforms are broken down and reshaped by weathering and erosion processes.
Content:
Weathering is the breakdown of rocks into smaller pieces through mechanical (physical) or chemical processes. Mechanical weathering includes frost action, thermal expansion, and biological activity. Chemical weathering involves processes like oxidation, carbonation, and hydration. Erosion is the removal and transportation of weathered materials by agents like water, wind, and ice. In Nigeria, the Harmattan wind causes mechanical weathering through abrasion. River erosion has created features like the Niger Delta and gorges in areas like the Mambilla Plateau. The processes of weathering and erosion work together to shape our landscape over time.
Class activity:
Students will observe and record examples of weathering and erosion in their local environment, taking photographs or making sketches.
Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between mechanical and chemical weathering.
2. Explain how the Harmattan wind contributes to weathering in Nigeria.
3. List three agents of erosion and their effects.
4. Describe how the Niger Delta was formed by river erosion.
Summary:
Weathering and erosion are continuous processes that gradually change the Earth's surface, creating the diverse landscapes we see in Nigeria and around the world.

topics.title: River systems
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the course of a river and its features.
The students should be able to explain how rivers shape the landscape.
Introduction:
Following our study of weathering and erosion, we will now focus specifically on rivers as one of the most powerful agents of erosion and deposition, examining their course, features, and influence on the landscape.
Content:
A river system consists of a main channel and all its tributaries. Rivers generally have three courses: upper (youthful), middle (mature), and lower (old). The upper course is characterized by V-shaped valleys, rapids, and waterfalls due to steep gradients and vertical erosion. The middle course has gentler slopes with meanders and oxbow lakes as lateral erosion becomes dominant. The lower course is nearly flat with wide floodplains and deltas due to deposition. In Nigeria, the River Niger has features like the Lokoja confluence where it meets the Benue River, and the Niger Delta formed by deposition. The River Kaduna also shows these characteristic features along its course.
Class activity:
Students will create a labeled diagram showing the features of a river in its three courses.
Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the characteristics of a river in its upper course.
2. Explain how meanders are formed in the middle course.
3. List three features of the lower course of a river.
4. Identify two major rivers in Nigeria and describe one feature of each.
Summary:
River systems play a crucial role in shaping Nigeria's landscape and providing water resources for agriculture, industry, and domestic use.

topics.title: Climate of Nigeria
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the climate regions of Nigeria.
The students should be able to explain the seasonal variations in Nigeria's climate.
Introduction:
We have studied various physical geographical features of Nigeria. Now we will focus on the climate, examining its different regions and the seasonal patterns that influence weather conditions across the country.
Content:
Nigeria has two main climate types: tropical monsoon and tropical savanna. The tropical monsoon climate is found in the south, characterized by high temperatures and heavy rainfall throughout the year with a short dry season. The tropical savanna climate is in the north, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The country experiences two main seasons: the rainy season (April-October) and the dry season (November-March). During the dry season, the Harmattan wind blows from the Sahara, bringing cool, dry dusty air. Temperature varies from the hot coastal areas to the cooler Jos Plateau and Mambilla Plateau. Rainfall decreases from south to north, with the south receiving over 2,000mm annually while the north receives less than 1,000mm.
Class activity:
Students will analyze climate data for different Nigerian cities to identify patterns and create climate graphs.
Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between the tropical monsoon and tropical savanna climates in Nigeria.
2. Explain the cause of the Harmattan season.
3. Describe the seasonal rainfall pattern in Nigeria.
4. How does altitude affect climate in Nigeria?
Summary:
Nigeria's climate varies from region to region, influenced by latitude, distance from the coast, and altitude, creating diverse environmental conditions across the country.

topics.title: Map reading
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to interpret contour lines on topographical maps.
The students should be able to calculate distance using map scale.
Introduction:
As we approach our final examinations, it is essential to strengthen our map reading skills. Today we will focus on interpreting contours and using scale to measure distances on topographical maps.
Content:
Contour lines are lines on a map joining points of equal elevation. The vertical distance between contour lines is called the contour interval. Close contour lines indicate steep slopes, while widely spaced lines show gentle slopes. Hachure marks (short lines) point downhill on some maps. Scale on maps shows the relationship between distances on the map and actual distances on the ground. We use the statement scale (1:50,000) or linear scale (graphical scale) to measure distances. In Nigeria, topographical maps use the UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) grid system for location. To calculate distance, we measure the map distance and multiply by the scale factor.
Class activity:
Students will practice interpreting contour maps by identifying landforms and calculating distances between points using the scale provided.
Evaluation questions:
1. What do closely spaced contour lines indicate on a topographical map?
2. Explain how to calculate the actual distance between two points on a map using a scale of 1:50,000.
3. Identify three landforms that can be recognized from contour patterns.
4. Describe the purpose of hachure marks on contour maps.
Summary:
Mastering contour interpretation and scale calculation is essential for success in map reading questions in our final examinations.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer WAEC-style questions accurately.
The students should be able to identify common mistakes in map interpretation.
Introduction:
As we conclude our term's work, we will engage in targeted revision and practice with past WAEC questions to prepare for the upcoming examinations.
Content:
We will focus on Paper 1 of the WAEC Geography examination, which consists of multiple-choice questions, map reading, and theory questions. We will practice interpreting topographical maps, calculating distances and gradients, and identifying geographical features. Students will learn to analyze questions carefully, identify key terms, and structure their answers appropriately. We will review common mistakes such as misinterpreting contour patterns, incorrect scale calculations, and inadequate explanations of geographical processes.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past WAEC questions and then present their answers to the class for discussion and correction.
Evaluation questions:
1. Calculate the gradient between two points A and B with an elevation difference of 50m and horizontal distance of 1km.
2. Identify the settlement pattern shown on the provided topographical map.
3. Explain the processes of river deposition with reference to the map.
4. Describe the factors influencing the location of settlements in the mapped area.
Summary:
Today's practice has helped us refine our examination techniques and identify areas that need further revision before our final examinations.
